newsitem.title: CANADA: Canadian auto workers strike GM.
newsitem.headline: Canadian auto workers strike GM.

text.p: More than 15,000 workers struck General Motors Corp. in Canada after contract talks foundered over the use of outside contractors, and the walkout could halt all of GM's Canadian operations by next week.

Talks resumed Thursday after the strike started late on Wednesday, but GM Canada said it had no plans to make a new contract offer to the Canadian Auto Workers union, meaning the the strike was likely to stretch at least into a second day.
"No, I don't think so," GM spokesman Stew Low said, when asked if a new offer would be made Thursday. "There's still a lot of talking to do to try to get things back on track."

The workers at GM's plants in Oshawa, Ontario, and Ste-Therese, Quebec, walked out hours before Wednesday's midnight strike deadline, after GM delivered a last-minute offer that CAW President Buzz Hargrove called an "insult."
Under the union's escalating strike strategy, other GM Canada plants were to join the strike on Sunday and all 26,000 union workers could be on strike by Wednesday if no deal was reached.

Analysts said that a strike by all GM union workers in Canada could cost the world's largest automaker $100 million to $150 million a week and eventually spill over and start forcing plants to shut down in the United States.

Separate talks continued between GM and the United Auto Workers union in the United States. UAW President Stephen Yokich said the union needs to make strategy decisions of its own and will confer with CAW leaders on how to proceed.

While talks resumed in Toronto, Hargrove said the two sides remained "worlds apart" on the major issue of outsourcing -- the use of outside, usually non-union workers -- as well as hours and work rule issues. He said he believes the Canadian talks were sunk by GM's Detroit headquarters.

"I think Detroit has put a halt to the bargaining," Hargrove told reporters after meeting with GM Canada lead negotiator Dean Munger Thursday. "We're on strike because someone (in Detroit) has failed to recognise that there is another country in this industry."

Hargrove said the strike would last until a contract was reached that mirrored the agreement the CAW and Chrysler Corp. reached on Sept. 17. That pact gave the CAW broad input into future decisions on outsourcing at Chrsyler.
"We'll stay out until the pattern is there," said Hargrove. "We are not leaving this bargaining until we have every word that is in the Chrysler job security language."
Munger said the strike would have a "severe impact" on GM Canada's operations but declined to speculate when the impact would reach U.S. operations or cripple GM's just-in-time parts supply strategy.
GM said earlier that a strike in Canada would not affect talks with the UAW in the United States. "We're working pretty much independently," GM spokesman Gerry Holmes said.

The CAW has said its C$50 million ($36.5 million) strike fund could last up to eight weeks and stretch to 16 weeks if new credit is arranged. The union has also set a special meeting for Oct. 18 to raise funds from the entire 210,000 membership of the CAW.
Workers at GM's St. Catharines, Ontario, engine and components plant were to join the strike on Oct. 6 and all Canadian operations will be shut down by Oct. 9 under the escalating strike plan.
More than 350 union leaders from plants across Ontario and Quebec were to meet on Friday in Toronto to discuss the negotiations and the strike.
Economists said that a prolonged strike against GM in Canada could hurt the country's fledgling economic recovery, shaving up to 1 point off growth in the fourth quarter.
"I think a short strike would have only a transitory effect, but a long one could be very damaging," said John McCallum, chief economist at Royal Bank of Canada in Toronto.
